✦ I Think, Therefore I Am ✦

René Descartes, the man who doubted everything, and the fly that gave us the coordinate plane

Chapter One · La Haye, France · 1596 to 1614

The Boy Who Stayed in Bed

René Descartes was born on 31 March 1596 in a small French town called La Haye en Touraine. (Today the town is named Descartes in his honour.) His mother died when he was still a baby, and he grew up thin, pale and often ill, with a dry cough. His father, a judge, is said to have called him his “little philosopher” because he asked questions about everything.

Around 1606, when René was about ten, he was sent to one of the best schools in Europe: the Jesuit college of La Flèche, founded by King Henri IV. For about eight years he studied Latin, Greek, logic, philosophy, and mathematics. The story goes that because he was so frail, the headmaster allowed him to stay in bed in the morning while the other boys went to class. It is told in a biography by Adrien Baillet, published in 1691, forty-one years after Descartes died, so treat it with care. What does seem true is that he kept the habit all his life. Lying warm in bed, thinking, was where he did his best work.

School left him unhappy in a strange way. He later wrote that the books taught him a great deal, but that on every question, the learned men disagreed. He observed that there is nothing so strange or hard to believe that some philosopher has not said it. If the cleverest people alive could not agree about anything, how was a student to know what was true?

There was one exception: mathematics. He wrote that he was delighted by it because of the certainty of its proofs. Nobody shouted about a triangle or about two plus two, and nobody stayed unconvinced once the steps were laid out. That was the feeling he wanted for the rest of knowledge. (If you read the Euclid lesson, you know exactly what he meant.)

He finished at La Flèche about 1614, studied law at the University of Poitiers, and earned his degree in 1616. Then he did something unusual for a young man with a law degree: he decided he had learned all he could from books, and that the rest of the learning would have to come from “the great book of the world.” He went out to see it.

🌟 Big Idea #1: When clever people disagree about everything, how do you decide what to believe? Descartes’s answer was to copy mathematics: accept only what you can see clearly for yourself, step by step.
★ Checkpoint 1 · La Flèche
Descartes arrived at the college of La Flèche around the year 1606 and left about 1614. About how many years did he spend there?
years
Subtract the start year from the finish year: 1614 − 1606.
Chapter Two · Breda and Germany · 1618 to 1619

A Soldier, a Stove, and Three Dreams

In 1618, the twenty-two-year-old Descartes joined the army of Prince Maurice of Nassau, in the Dutch town of Breda. He was a gentleman-volunteer, not much of a fighter. There was a pause in the war at the time, and the young Frenchman had plenty of free hours.

One story, again from Baillet, says that he saw a crowd reading a poster in Dutch, a language he did not know. The poster was a maths puzzle. He asked a bystander to translate it into French or Latin. The bystander turned out to be Isaac Beeckman, a Dutch scientist and schoolmaster, who set him a harder problem as a joke. Descartes is said to have solved it in a few hours. True or not, the two did become close friends, and Beeckman reawakened Descartes’s love of mathematics and of explaining nature with numbers.

The next year the great religious war that we now call the Thirty Years’ War was blazing, and Descartes joined another army, in Germany. On 10 November 1619, snowed in at winter quarters near the Danube, he shut himself into a room heated by a large stove. That night, as he later recorded in a notebook, he had three vivid dreams. He came away convinced that he had found “the foundations of a wonderful science.” The notebook is lost. We know of it only through Baillet’s summary seventy years later, so the details are uncertain. What we do know is that this was the moment he decided what to do with his life.

Where did the idea come from? Look at what mathematicians do. They take a huge, scary problem and cut it into small steps, each so simple that nobody can doubt it. Then they chain the steps together. Descartes noticed that this is exactly how Euclid proved everything. Why not use the same chain for all questions? He later wrote it down as four short rules in his Discourse on Method (1637):

1. Accept nothing as true unless you see it so clearly that you cannot doubt it.
2. Divide each difficulty into as many small parts as you can.
3. Think in order, starting with the simplest things and climbing step by step to the complex ones.
4. Check everything so thoroughly, with lists and reviews, that you are sure nothing has been missed.

Rule 2 is the one you will use most. Here it is on a multiplication problem. To work out 13 × 15, don’t try to do it all at once. Split 15 into 10 + 5. Then 13 × 10 = 130, and 13 × 5 = 65, and the answer is 130 + 65 = 195. A hard thing became two easy things.

★ Checkpoint 2 · Rule 2 · divide the difficulty
Use Descartes’s second rule. Split 24 into 20 + 4 and work out 17 × 24.
17 × 20 = 340, and 17 × 4 = 68. Add the two pieces together.
Chapter Three · The Netherlands · the 1630s and 1640s

Can I Trust My Eyes?

In 1628 Descartes moved to the Dutch Republic, and there he stayed, with a few moves from town to town, for about twenty years. The Dutch Republic was one of the freest and busiest places in Europe. It had printing presses, good lenses, and few people watching what you thought. He liked it so much that he said he walked through the crowds of Amsterdam as calmly as if he were walking in a forest.

Here he began the project that made him famous, and it started with a very odd job: doubting everything he could. The idea is easiest to see with a basket of apples. Suppose you have a basket, and you fear some of the apples are rotten. The sensible thing to do is to tip them all out, look at each one, and put back only the good ones. In his mind, Descartes tipped out every belief he had and put back only those that survived.

First to go were beliefs that come from the senses. A stick half in water looks bent, but it is straight. A square tower seen from far away looks round. Your eyes have fooled you before, and he thought it unwise to trust completely something that has ever fooled you.

But surely, he thought, I can trust my senses about things that are right in front of me, such as that I am sitting here by the fire with a paper in my hand? Then he stopped himself. His own words, from the Meditations on First Philosophy (1641): how often, asleep at night, am I sure of just such familiar facts, that I am sitting by the fire in my dressing gown, when in fact I am lying undressed in bed! In a dream, everything feels real. And he could find no sure sign that would tell waking from dreaming.

That is the dream argument. Think about how much time is involved. You spend about one-third of your life asleep. If dreams can feel real, and you spend a third of your life in them, can you be sure you are not dreaming right now?

🔎 About 1,900 years earlier, the Chinese thinker Zhuangzi told of dreaming he was a butterfly, and waking up unsure whether he was a man who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was a man. The puzzle is very old. Descartes made it sharp.

You are probably thinking, “But this is silly. I know I’m awake!” Descartes would nod. He did not believe he was dreaming. He used the idea like a crowbar to test which beliefs would hold up if someone pushed hard. In everyday life, he said, you should keep acting normally, eat dinner, and go to bed. The doubt was something he did in his study, on purpose, for a short time.

★ Checkpoint 3 · The dream argument
Suppose a person sleeps 8 hours out of every 24, which is one-third of their time. If they live to be 75, how many years of their life do they spend asleep?
years
One-third of 75 is 75 ÷ 3.
Chapter Four · Meditation One

The Evil Demon

The dream argument shook the senses. But what about things you know without looking at anything? Surely 2 + 3 = 5, and a square has four sides, whether I am dreaming or awake. These are as safe as anything can be.

Descartes was not satisfied. He imagined something stranger and more frightening. His words: suppose that some malicious demon of the utmost power and cunning has used all of his energy to deceive me. Suppose the sky, the air, the earth, colours, shapes and sounds are nothing but tricks the demon uses to catch my belief. I will think of myself as having no hands, no eyes, no flesh, and no blood. This is the evil demon (he also called it a “malicious genius”), and it is one of the most famous thought experiments in history.

What could the demon do to mathematics? Descartes pushed the thought as far as it would go. If a demon were powerful enough, it might arrange for you to go wrong every single time you add two and three, or count the sides of a square. There would be no feeling of being wrong. The mistake would look perfectly clear to you. So even sums could be doubted.

This idea has come back many times. In 1981 the American philosopher Hilary Putnam asked what if you were a brain in a vat, fed all of your experiences by a computer. Movies like The Matrix use the same thought. All of them go back to Descartes’s demon.

Why would anyone do this to themselves? Remember the apple basket. Descartes wanted a foundation that nothing could shake, not even a demon. If he could find one single thing that survived all of this, he could build everything else on it. If he could not, then all his knowledge was sand. It was a test of strength, applied as hard as he could.

🔎 Descartes did not stay in the dark forever. After he found his first solid fact, he went on to argue that a good God exists and would not let him be tricked all the time. Many readers, then and now, think that step is the weakest part of his chain. Even his friends argued with him about it. Descartes would have been the first to tell you to check his work.

A practical lesson from the demon is that when something matters, you should check it a second way. If a demon might be rigging your adding, add in a different order, or subtract to see if you get back to where you started.

★ Checkpoint 4 · Doubting the sum
Descartes would say: check your work by a second route. Work out 478 + 356. Then check by adding 356 to 478 the other way round (or subtract to get back).
478 + 300 = 778. Then 778 + 56 = 834. Check: 834 − 356 should give 478.
Chapter Five · Discourse Part 4 and Meditation Two

I Think, Therefore I Am

Now Descartes had thrown away the senses, the body, the sky, even arithmetic. Was anything left? He went hunting for any single fact that the demon could not touch.

Then he saw it. Suppose the demon is tricking me about everything. Then there must be a me that is being tricked. To be fooled, I have to exist. The more power the demon uses to deceive me, the more certain it becomes that I am here. In the Meditations he wrote that the statement “I am, I exist” is necessarily true each time I say it or think it.

Put into one sentence, that is the most famous line in philosophy. It first appeared in print in French in the Discourse on Method (1637): “Je pense, donc je suis.” In 1644, in the Latin Principles of Philosophy, it became the version we know best: “Cogito, ergo sum.” In English: I think, therefore I am.

Notice how modest the claim is. He had not proved the sky exists, or his body, or other people. He had found only that there is thinking going on, so there is a thinker. He wrote that his “I” at this stage was only “a thing that thinks”: something that doubts, understands, affirms, denies, wishes, imagines and feels. It was a tiny island. But he said it was solid, and he would build on it.

That is exactly what Euclid does with a few postulates. A system of knowledge needs a point where you stand. Descartes found his.

🔎 Was Descartes the first to think of it? No. About AD 420, Saint Augustine wrote “si fallor, sum”: if I am mistaken, I am. Descartes’s contemporaries pointed this out to him. He answered politely that he had not read the passage, and that he used the idea for a different purpose: not to prove the soul, but to begin a whole new chain of knowledge from scratch.

Count how the demolition went. He began with a long list of things he believed. The senses fell to the dream argument. The body fell with them. Mathematics fell to the demon. What stood at the end was a very short list.

🌟 Big Idea #2: A certain starting point is worth more than a thousand likely guesses. Find one thing you cannot doubt, then build outward with clear steps, checking each one.
★ Checkpoint 5 · What is left standing?
Descartes starts with 10 beliefs on his list. The dream argument knocks out 4 (beliefs from the senses). The loss of the body knocks out 3 more. The evil demon knocks out 2 (the mathematics). How many beliefs survive? (It is the one he is famous for.)
belief
10 − 4 − 3 − 2. What is left over?
Chapter Six · The Legend

The Fly on the Ceiling

Now to the story you came for. The story goes that Descartes was lying in bed one morning, as usual, with nothing to do but think. A fly was crawling about on the ceiling. He watched it. And a question formed: how could I tell someone exactly where that fly is?

You could say “near the lamp.” But that is vague. You could say “a hand’s width from the window.” Better, but whose hand? Then he realised: pick one corner of the ceiling. Two walls meet there. Measure how far the fly is along one wall. Then measure how far it is along the other wall. Two numbers, and the fly’s position is exactly fixed. The fly could crawl anywhere, and at every moment you could describe where it was with just two numbers.

The path of the fly, then, is a list of number pairs. If the fly moves in a straight line, the numbers follow a pattern. If it moves in a circle, they follow a different pattern. The pattern is an equation. That is the secret. A shape becomes a rule, and a rule becomes a shape.

🔎 Is the fly story true? Probably not as told. The story is repeated in many books, but we cannot find it in Descartes’s own writings, and we do not know who first told it. Historians of mathematics also note that Descartes did not write coordinates as modern number pairs. The real idea is unmistakable in his book, though. The fly is a good way to remember the idea, and the project’s rule is to call a story a story.

Mathematicians now write a fly’s address as an ordered pair, (x, y). The first number is always across (x), and the second is always along (y). Order matters: (4, 2) is not the same spot as (2, 4). The corner where you start is called the origin, and its address is (0, 0).

The pair of measuring lines is called a Cartesian plane, after Descartes’s Latin name, Cartesius. (A “plane” here means a flat surface that goes on as far as you like.) Try the fly yourself. Click on the ceiling, or use the sliders, and watch the address change. Move the fly several times and the trail it leaves is a path made of addresses.

The ceiling corner · click to move the fly

Once you have addresses, you can ask: how far apart are two spots? If the fly walks straight along a row, it is easy. You just subtract. If it walks diagonally, imagine a right triangle: one leg across, one leg along. The fly’s straight path is the hypotenuse. That is Pythagoras: a² + b² = c². Descartes was combining two ancient ideas, the grid and the right triangle, and they fit together perfectly.

★ Checkpoint 6 · Distance along a row
A fly sits at A = (1, 2) and crawls straight along the row to B = (4, 2). How many steps did it crawl?
steps
Both spots are on the same row (y = 2). Only the x-number changes: 4 − 1.
★ Checkpoint 7 · Distance on a diagonal
Now a fly crawls in a straight line from A = (1, 1) to B = (4, 5). The dashed lines make a right triangle. How many steps long is the straight path AB?
steps
The legs are 4 − 1 = 3 across and 5 − 1 = 4 up. Then 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, and the square root of 25 is 5.

Chapter Seven · La Géométrie · 1637

Where Algebra Met Geometry

In 1637, Descartes published his first book. Its full title was long: Discourse on the Method of Rightly Conducting One’s Reason and Seeking Truth in the Sciences. Three “essays” followed it as examples of the method at work: one on optics (La Dioptrique), one on weather (Les Météores), and one on geometry: La Géométrie. It was printed in the Dutch city of Leiden, in French instead of Latin, so that ordinary educated readers could follow, and his name did not appear on the title page.

Before this book, geometry and algebra lived in separate houses. Geometry was about shapes, drawn with ruler and compass, like Euclid’s. Algebra was about unknown numbers and rules for finding them. Few people thought of using one to help the other.

Descartes connected them. Pick a reference line. Then a point on a curve can be described by how far along the line it is, and how far away from the line it is. Call these two lengths x and y. A curve is simply every point where x and y obey some rule. An equation that mixes x and y is a description of a curve. And if you can describe a curve by an equation, you can solve geometry problems with algebra, without drawing a thing.

He also tidied up how maths is written. He used letters from the start of the alphabet (a, b, c) for numbers that are known, and letters from the end (x, y, z) for the unknowns. That habit has stuck for nearly 400 years. He wrote powers with small raised numbers, such as x³, for x × x × x. Before him, maths was often written in long sentences.

The French lawyer and mathematician Pierre de Fermat had the same idea at about the same time, working alone. Fermat did not publish his, so the credit went to Descartes. And Descartes’s own plane was not quite the modern one. He mostly used distances measured in one direction, and the full picture with two axes crossing at the middle and negative numbers going left and down was filled in by those who came after him. Isaac Newton studied the Latin edition of La Géométrie as a student, and he helped carry the idea forward.

Play with the plane below. Move the sliders and watch an equation draw a line, or draw a circle. Notice the four quadrants. In the top left, x is negative (it is to the left of the middle). In the bottom right, y is negative (below the middle).

The plane · an equation draws a picture

A line has the form y = mx + b. The number b says where the line crosses the up-down axis, and m says how steeply it climbs. Take the line y = 2x + 1. When x = 0, y = 1. When x = 1, y = 3. When x = 2, y = 5. Every time x goes up by 1, y goes up by 2.

A circle centred on the origin has the form x² + y² = r², where r is the radius. This is Pythagoras again. A point (x, y) is exactly r steps from the origin when x² + y² = r². For example, (3, 4) is on the circle with r = 5, because 9 + 16 = 25.

Put 3 in place of x: 2 × 3 + 1.

Ignore the minus sign for the distance: the legs are 6 and 8. Then 36 + 64 = 100.

Using his habit of writing powers, find the value of x² − 2x when x = 5.
x² means x × x, which is 25. Then 2x is 10. Subtract.
Chapter Eight · Egmond, Stockholm · 1633 to 1650

The Man Who Hid

In 1633, Descartes was nearly finished with a book called The World, which explained the universe as a machine, with the Earth moving around the Sun. Then news came from Italy: the Church had put Galileo on trial for saying exactly that, and had forced him to take it back. Descartes put The World in a drawer. It was not printed until after he died. He kept as his motto a line of the Roman poet Ovid: bene vixit, bene qui latuit, “he lives well who hides well.” (A note in his early papers read, larvatus prodeo: “masked, I advance.”)

Still, his ideas got out. He wrote in 1641 the Meditations, and in 1644 the Principles of Philosophy. He compared all knowledge to a tree: the roots are the first questions (what can I be sure of?), the trunk is physics, and the branches are the useful sciences, such as medicine and mechanics.

He also defended a strong idea about the mind and the body: that they are two different kinds of thing, one made of thought and the other of matter. A clever young woman, Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, wrote him letters from 1643 asking the hard question: if the mind is not a physical thing, how can it move the body? He did not have a good answer, and they kept writing.

In 1649, Queen Christina of Sweden, who was only twenty-two and fiercely eager to learn, invited him to Stockholm to teach her. He went. The tale told is that she wanted her lessons at five in the morning, in a cold library, and that the late-sleeping philosopher, now in a Swedish winter, caught pneumonia. He died on 11 February 1650, aged 53. (Some historians have wondered whether the story is exaggerated, but the sudden death in a northern winter is a fact.)

Here are the words he is best remembered for. They come from his books and letters, but he wrote in French and Latin, so the English is a translation.

Lines he is remembered for
  1. “I think, therefore I am.” (Je pense, donc je suis, Discourse on Method, 1637; Cogito, ergo sum, Principles of Philosophy, 1644.) The one fact the demon cannot take away.
  2. “It is not enough to have a good mind; the main thing is to use it well.” (Discourse, Part 1.) Brains are not the scarce thing. Method is.
  3. “Divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible.” (Discourse, Part 2.) His second rule of method, and the engine of all later science.
  4. “It is necessary, once in the course of our life, to doubt, as far as possible, all things.” (Principles of Philosophy, Part 1, 1644.) Doubt as a one-time house-cleaning, not a way of life.
  5. “The reading of all good books is like a conversation with the finest minds of past centuries.” (Discourse, Part 1.)
  6. “Good sense is the best shared thing in the world.” (The opening line of the Discourse.) He added, with a straight face, that everyone is sure they already have enough of it.
  7. “Always try to master myself rather than fortune, and to change my desires rather than the order of the world.” (Discourse, Part 3.)
  8. Larvatus prodeo: “Masked, I advance.” (A note from his early private papers, around 1619.)
  9. Bene vixit, bene qui latuit: “He lives well who hides well.” (A line of the Roman poet Ovid, which Descartes took to heart after Galileo’s trial.)
Descartes wrote in French and Latin, so every English version is a translation. Wording varies a little from book to book.

After he died, the word Cartesian came to mean both his philosophy and his grid. Even now, when you find a spot on a map by two numbers, or plot a graph in science class, you are using his idea.

★ Checkpoint 13 · A lifetime of ideas
Descartes published La Géométrie in 1637 and died in 1650. How many years after the book appeared did he die?
years

Epilogue

✦ One Sure Point, and a Grid to Put It On ✦

Look at the two things Descartes left us, side by side. One is a way of thinking: doubt everything you can, find the single thing you cannot doubt, and then build upward one careful step at a time. The other is a way of drawing: pick a corner, measure two distances, and every spot in the world gets a two-number address. They are really the same idea. Both start from one fixed point (I think, or the corner of the ceiling) and both build a whole world from there by clear, checkable steps.

The grid changed science more than the doubt did. Once any curve can be written as an equation, you can describe the path of a cannonball, a planet, or a stock price with a rule, and then use algebra to answer questions about it. Isaac Newton studied Descartes’s geometry as a student at Cambridge. When Newton worked out the orbit of the Moon, he was walking on the road Descartes had paved. Every graph in every textbook, every map on your phone, every video game that places a character at (x, y), is a descendant of that idea.

The doubt did not disappear either. Whenever someone asks “how do you know?” and will not accept “because everyone says so,” that is Descartes in the room. He would also want you to remember the second half of his method, which is easy to forget: after you doubt, you rebuild. Doubt is the demolition. Reasoning is the construction.

And the fly? Maybe it was there, maybe it was not. The story is probably a tale told long after his death. But you have just spent a lesson placing a fly at (4, 2), crawling it to (4, 5), and measuring the distance with the Pythagorean theorem. Whoever the first person was who thought of it, you now think like them.

⭐ Master of the Grid ⭐

What you now know that most adults don't:

① Descartes (1596 to 1650) set out to doubt everything he could and keep only what survived. His method has four rules, the second being to divide every difficulty into as many parts as needed.

② The dream argument and the evil demon were thought experiments. He did not believe he was being tricked. He wanted to see what was left standing.

③ The one thing left was “I think, therefore I am”: even a deceived mind must exist to be deceived. (Saint Augustine had a similar thought 1,200 years earlier.)

④ The fly on the ceiling is a legend, but its idea is real. A point's position can be given by two numbers, such as (4, 2), and the distance between two points comes from a² + b² = c².

⑤ La Géométrie (1637) joined algebra to geometry: an equation such as y = 2x + 1 or x² + y² = 25 draws a line or a circle on the plane.

⑥ The plane is called Cartesian after his Latin name, Cartesius. Negative numbers and all four quadrants came into general use after him.
